tea:bhagavad-gita:2.60.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:2.60.original:
yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ|
indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṃ manaḥ
tea:bhagavad-gita:2.60.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: for the turbulent (pramāthin) senses, son of Kuntī, forcibly carry off the mind (manas) even of a discerning person (vipaścit) who is striving.

tea:bhagavad-gita:2.67.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:2.67.original:
indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano'nuvidhīyate|
tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi
tea:bhagavad-gita:2.67.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: for when the mind (manas) is led along by the roving senses, it carries off his wisdom (prajñā), as the wind carries off a ship on the water.

tea:bhagavad-gita:5.22.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:5.22.original:
ye hi saṃsparśajā bhogā duḥkhayonaya eva te|
ādyantavantaḥ kaunteya na teṣu ramate budhaḥ
tea:bhagavad-gita:5.22.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: for the enjoyments (bhoga) born of contact (saṃsparśa) are wombs of sorrow (duḥkha); they have a beginning and an end, son of Kuntī; the wise one does not delight in them.

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.11.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.11.original:
śucau deśe pratiṣṭhāpya sthiramāsanamātmanaḥ|
nātyucchritaṃ nātinīcaṃ cailājinakuśottaram
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.11.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: having set up for himself, in a clean place, a firm seat (āsana), neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deer-skin and kuśa grass,

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.13.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.13.original:
samaṃ kāyaśirogrīvaṃ dhārayannacalaṃ sthiraḥ|
saṃprekṣya nāsikāgraṃ svaṃ diśaścānavalokayan
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.13.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: [continuing 6.12] holding body, head and neck in line (sama) and motionless, steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose (nāsikāgra) and not looking about in the directions,

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.16.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.16.original:
nātyaśnatastu yogo'sti na caikāntamanaśnataḥ|
na cātisvapnaśīlasya jāgrato naiva cārjuna
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.16.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one given to too much sleep, nor for one who keeps (always) awake, Arjuna.

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.17.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.17.original:
yuktāhāravihārasya yuktaceṣṭasya karmasu|
yuktasvapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkhahā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.17.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: for one who is measured (yukta) in food and recreation (āhāra-vihāra), measured in exertion in actions, measured in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering (duḥkhahā).

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.23.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.23.original:
taṃ vidyād duḥkhasaṃyogaviyogaṃ yogasaṃjñitam|
sa niścayena yoktavyo yogo'nirviṇṇacetasā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.23.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: [continuing 6.22] that one should know as what is called yoga: the unyoking from union with sorrow (duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyoga). This yoga is to be practised with resolve (niścaya) and with an undejected mind (anirviṇṇa-cetas).

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.25.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.25.original:
śanaiḥ śanairuparamed buddhyā dhṛtigṛhītayā|
ātmasaṃsthaṃ manaḥ kṛtvā na kiñcidapi cintayet
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.25.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: [continuing 6.24] one should come to rest (uparamet) little by little, by the intellect (buddhi) held in steadfastness (dhṛti); having made the mind abide in the self (ātma-saṃstha), one should think of nothing at all (na kiṃcid api cintayet).

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.26.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.26.original:
yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram|
tatastato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.26.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: wherever the restless (cañcala), unsteady mind wanders off, from there he should restrain it and bring it back under control in the self alone.

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.34.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.34.original:
cañcalaṃ hi manaḥ kṛṣṇa pramāthi balavaddṛḍham|
tasyāhaṃ nigrahaṃ manye vāyoriva suduṣkaram
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.34.paraphrase: Arjuna: for the mind is restless, Kṛṣṇa, turbulent (pramāthin), strong and obstinate (dṛḍha); I think restraining it (nigraha) is as very hard as restraining the wind.

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.35.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.35.original:
śrī bhagavānuvāca
asaṃśayaṃ mahābāho mano durnigrahaṃ calaṃ|
abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.35.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: without doubt, mighty-armed, the mind is hard to restrain and restless; but by practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya), son of Kuntī, it is held (gṛhyate).

tea:bhagavad-gita:6.36.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.36.original:
asaṃyatātmanā yogo duṣprāpa iti me matiḥ|
vaśyātmanā tu yatatā śakyo'vāptumupāyataḥ
tea:bhagavad-gita:6.36.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is unrestrained — this is my view; but by one whose self is under control and who strives, it can be attained through the right means (upāya).

tea:mahasatipatthana-sutta:dn22:13.title: Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta
tea:mahasatipatthana-sutta:dn22:13.original: 4. Dhammānupassanā 4.1. Dhammānupassanānīvaraṇapabba Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa kāmacchandassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa kāmacchandassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa byāpādassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa byāpādassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa byāpādassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa thinamiddhassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa thinamiddhassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa uddhaccakukkuccassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannāya vicikicchāya uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannāya vicikicchāya pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnāya vicikicchāya āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Iti ajjhattaṁ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya, anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu. Nīvaraṇapabbaṁ niṭṭhitaṁ.
tea:mahasatipatthana-sutta:dn22:13.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, first section: the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). A monk knows sensual desire (kāmacchanda) present in him as present and absent as absent; he knows how unarisen sensual desire comes to arise, how arisen sensual desire is abandoned, and how the abandoned will not arise again in the future. He does the same for ill will (byāpāda), dullness and drowsiness (thina-middha), restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) and doubt (vicikicchā). The refrain follows in full and the hindrances section ends.

tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:34.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:34.original: 3. Cittānupassanā Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sarāgaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘sarāgaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vītarāgaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vītarāgaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Sadosaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘sadosaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vītadosaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vītadosaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Samohaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘samohaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vītamohaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vītamohaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Saṅkhittaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘saṅkhittaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vikkhittaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vikkhittaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Mahaggataṁ vā cittaṁ ‘mahaggataṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Amahaggataṁ vā cittaṁ ‘amahaggataṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Sauttaraṁ vā cittaṁ ‘sauttaraṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Anuttaraṁ vā cittaṁ ‘anuttaraṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Samāhitaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘samāhitaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Asamāhitaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘asamāhitaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vimuttaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vimuttaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Avimuttaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘avimuttaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti.
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:34.paraphrase: Contemplation of mind (citta). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating mind in mind. Here he knows a mind with lust (sarāga) as 'mind with lust', and a mind without lust as 'mind without lust'; a mind with hatred (sadosa) and without hatred; a mind with delusion (samoha) and without delusion; a contracted (saṅkhitta) mind and a scattered (vikkhitta) mind; an exalted (mahaggata) and an unexalted mind; a surpassable (sauttara) and an unsurpassable (anuttara) mind; a concentrated (samāhita) and an unconcentrated mind; a liberated (vimutta) and an unliberated mind.

tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:36.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:36.original: 4. Dhammānupassanā 4.1. Dhammānupassanānīvaraṇapabba Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa kāmacchandassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa kāmacchandassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa byāpādassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa byāpādassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa byāpādassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa thinamiddhassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa thinamiddhassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa uddhaccakukkuccassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannāya vicikicchāya uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannāya vicikicchāya pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnāya vicikicchāya āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:36.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, first section: the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating dhammas in dhammas with regard to the five hindrances. Here, when sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is present in him he knows 'there is sensual desire in me'; when it is absent he knows 'there is no sensual desire in me'; he knows how unarisen sensual desire comes to arise; he knows how arisen sensual desire is abandoned; and he knows how the abandoned sensual desire will not arise again in the future. He does the same, in exactly this fivefold way, for ill will (byāpāda), for dullness and drowsiness (thina-middha), for restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) and for doubt (vicikicchā).

tea:visuddhimagga:14.p469.original:

ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādipadaṭṭhānā, paramaṃ vajjan  
ti daṭṭhabbā1|  
     uddhatabhāvo uddhaccaṃ| taṃ avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ,  
vātābhighātacalajalaṃ viya anavaṭṭhānarasaṃ, vātābhi-  
ghātacaladhajapaṭākā viya, bhantattapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, pā-  
sāṇābhighātasamuddhatabhasmaṃ viya, cetaso avūpasame  
ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ, cittavikkhepo ti daṭṭhab-  
baṃ|

cupaṭṭhānaṃ pacalāyikāniddāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā; ubhayam  
pi arativijambhikādisu ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ|  
     tatiyena paṭhame vuttesu, ṭhapetvā micchādiṭṭhiṃ, ava-  
sesā veditabbā| māno pan'; ettha aniyato hoti| ayaṃ viseso:  
so uṇṇatilakkhaṇo, sampaggaharaso, ketukamyatāpaccupaṭ-  
ṭhāno, diṭṭhivippayuttalobhapadaṭṭhāno, ummādo viya daṭ-  
ṭhabbo| catutthena dutiye vuttesu, ṭhapetvā micchādiṭ-  
ṭhiṃ, avasesā veditabbā| etthā pi ca māno aniyatesu hoti

diṭṭhiṃ, avasesā veditabbā| māno pan'; ettha aniyato hoti|

tabbā| etthā pi ca māno aniyatesu hoti yevā ti| dosamūlesu
tea:visuddhimagga:14.p469.paraphrase: Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is that by which one sees wrongly, or which sees wrongly, or mere wrong seeing: its mark is unwise insistence; its function is clinging; its manifestation is wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the wish not to see the noble ones and the like; it is to be regarded as the most blameworthy. Restlessness (uddhacca) is agitated state: its mark is non-calming; its function is unsteadiness, like water stirred by wind; its manifestation is bewilderment, like a flag fluttering in the wind or like ashes thrown up by a blow on a stone; its proximate cause is unwise attention to the non-calming of the mind; it is to be regarded as distraction of consciousness. The other factors are as stated for the unwholesome. The second unwholesome consciousness is like the first, but prompted and with sloth-torpor indeterminate. Sloth (thīna) is the sinking, torpor (middha) the drowsing: sloth has as its mark lack of energy and as function dispelling energy, as manifestation sinking; torpor has as mark unworkableness, as function smothering, as manifestation drooping or drowsy sleep; for both the proximate cause is unwise attention to discontent, lazy stretching and the like. Conceit (māna), indeterminate in the third and fourth, has as mark haughtiness, as function self-promotion, as manifestation vain-glory, as proximate cause greed dissociated from view; it is to be regarded as madness. The fifth to eighth are given in the same manner without wrong view or with joy left out.

tea:visuddhimagga:22.p682.title: Visuddhimagga
tea:visuddhimagga:22.p682.original:

ṭhāti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehi vuṭṭhāti, tena vuccati: dubhato  
vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā magge ñāṇan ti2|  
     lokiyānañ ca aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ bhāvanākāle sam-  
athabalaṃ adhikaṃ hoti; aniccānupassanādīnaṃ bhāvanā-  
kāle vipassanābalaṃ| ariyamaggakhaṇe pana yuganandhā

tea:visuddhimagga:22.p682.paraphrase: At the moment of the arahat path he emerges from the remaining fetters and latent tendencies (from lust for fine-material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance; the latent conceit, latent lust for existence, latent ignorance), from the defilements that follow them and the aggregates, and outwardly from all signs: as quoted, "understanding in the turning away by emerging in both ways is knowledge in the path". In the development of the eight worldly attainments calm is stronger; in developing the contemplation of impermanence and so on, insight is stronger; in the moment of the noble path they occur yoked together, neither exceeding the other; so in the four knowledges of the paths there is a joining of both powers. The text quotes the Paṭisambhidā: for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by restlessness and from the aggregates, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration whose domain is cessation; for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by ignorance, insight in the sense of contemplation has cessation as domain; thus in the sense of emerging calm and insight are of one taste, yoked and not exceeding each other. Then, under "what is to be abandoned by which, and the abandoning", the text begins: in these four knowledges one should know what states are to be abandoned by each knowledge, states that come as fetters, defilements, wrongnesses, worldly conditions, avarice, perversions, ties, wrong courses, taints, floods, yokes, hindrances, adherences, clingings, latent tendencies, stains, unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome thoughts. Fetters are ten things that bind beings to aggregates, to the fruit of kamma and to suffering; of them five are higher fetters (lust for fine-material existence, for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance) (continued on p. 683).

tea:yoga-bhasya:1.1.title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)
tea:yoga-bhasya:1.1.original:
athety ayam adhikārārthaḥ /
yogānuśāsanaṃ śāstram adhikṛtaṃ veditavyam /
yogaḥ samādhiḥ /
sa ca sārvabhaumaś cittasya dharmaḥ /
kṣiptaṃ mūḍhaṃ vikṣiptam ekāgraṃ niruddham iti cittabhūmayaḥ /
tatra vikṣipte cetasi vikṣepopasarjanībhūtaḥ samādhir na yogapakṣe vartate /
yas tv ekāgre cetasi sadbhūtam arthaṃ pradyotayati kṣiṇoti ca kleśān karmabandhanāni ślathayati nirodham abhimukhaṃ karoti sa saṃprajñāto yoga ity ākhyāyate /
sa ca vitarkānugato vicārānugata ānandānugato 'smitānugata ity upariṣṭān nivedayiṣyāmaḥ /
sarvavṛttinirodhe tv asaṃprajñātaḥ samādhiḥ
tea:yoga-bhasya:1.1.paraphrase: 'Now' (atha) marks that a topic is taken up (adhikāra): the treatise called 'the teaching of yoga' is to be understood as the subject in hand. Yoga is samādhi, and samādhi is a property of the mind (citta) at every level (sārvabhauma). The levels of the mind (citta-bhūmi) are: scattered (kṣipta), stupefied (mūḍha), distracted (vikṣipta), one-pointed (ekāgra) and stilled (niruddha). In a distracted mind, samādhi that has become subordinate to the distraction does not count on the side of yoga. But in the one-pointed mind, the samādhi that illumines the real object (sadbhūta artha), wears away the afflictions (kleśa), loosens the bonds of karma and turns the mind toward stilling (nirodha) is called samprajñāta yoga. That samādhi is accompanied by reasoning (vitarka), by reflection (vicāra), by joy (ānanda) or by I-am-ness (asmitā) — Vyāsa says he will set this out later. In the stilling of all activities, samādhi is asamprajñāta.

summary: You described a pattern that the texts name: Cañcala manas (the restless mind), in the Vedic/yogic texts. Each is shown below with your own words and the texts' description.

points.text: Your words “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine” may fit what the Vedic and yogic texts call Cañcala manas (the restless mind). Arjuna: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate; I think it as hard to hold as the wind (BhG 6.34). Kṛṣṇa: no doubt the mind is hard to hold and moving, but it is held by practice and dispassion (6.35). The turbulent senses carry off by force the mind even of a wise man who strives (2.60); the mind that follows the roving senses carries off understanding as the wind a ship on the water (2.67).

The Buddhist texts have their own account of a pattern like the one above: Uddhacca-kukkucca (restlessness and remorse) (a partial match for Cañcala manas (the restless mind)). Contemplating dhammas as the five hindrances: when restlessness and remorse is present in him the monk knows 'there is restlessness and remorse in me'; when absent, 'there is no restlessness and remorse in me'; he knows how the unarisen restlessness and remorse arises, how the arisen restlessness and remorse is abandoned, and how the abandoned restlessness and remorse does not arise again. Your words were matched to Cañcala manas (the restless mind), not to this; it is shown so that both readings are in view.

Each names a mind that will not stay. Gītā: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (BhG 6.34). It is held by practice and dispassion (BhG 6.35), and wherever it wanders it is to be brought back (BhG 6.26). Vyāsa: samādhi is a property of the mind at every level, and one of its grounds is the distracted (vikṣipta) (YB 1.1). Suttas: restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) is a hindrance known as present or absent (MN 10:36), and a scattered (vikkhitta) mind is known as scattered (MN 10:34). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.

differences.text: (1) Vyāsa's distracted mind is one ground in a scale of grounds of mind (YB 1.1). MN 10 only names the scattered mind as something to be known, with no scale (MN 10:34). (2) The hindrance joins restlessness and remorse (kukkucca) into one (MN 10:36). The Gītā passage speaks of restlessness alone. (3) The Gītā names the remedy, practice and dispassion (BhG 6.35). MN 10's approach in this passage is to know the hindrance as present, arising and abandoned (MN 10:36). (4) The Visuddhimagga defines restlessness by its mark of non-calming (Vism XIV). It counts restlessness among the fetters that remain until the arahat path (Vism XXII), a depth that the Gītā and Vyāsa passages do not grade.

practices.name: Practice and dispassion (abhyāsa, vairāgya, BhG 6.35)
practices.why: You wrote “At night my mind runs like a sewing machine”. This reading suggests the practice below for what the texts call Cañcala manas (the restless mind); the practice comes from the texts cited with it, and the pairing is this reading's, not theirs.
steps: Sit on a firm seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low (BhG 6.11), body, head and neck in line and still (6.13).
Practice (abhyāsa): wherever the restless mind wanders off, restrain it from there and bring it back (6.26).
Dispassion (vairāgya): recall that enjoyments born of contact have a beginning and an end and are wombs of sorrow; the wise one does not delight in them (5.22).
Come to rest little by little (śanaiḥ śanaiḥ), not all at once (6.25).

warnings.text: Moderation: yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one who sleeps too much or keeps always awake; it is for one measured in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking.
The Gītā asks that yoga be practised with resolve and with an undejected mind (anirviṇṇa-cetas).
The Gītā grants that the mind is hard to restrain; it is held by practice and dispassion (6.35), and yoga can be attained by one who strives through the right means (6.36).
